questions.stem: In a novel, a round character is one who:
options: tells the whole story in the first person, using I
is complex, with sides that can surprise the reader
appears only briefly and is defined by one single trait
is always the villain who works against the hero
questions.explanation: A round character is drawn in depth, with mixed qualities, contradictions and a believable inner life. A character defined by one trait is the opposite, a flat character. Round characters can be heroes, villains or anyone else, and they can appear in any kind of narration.

questions.stem: In a detective novel, the grumpy café owner appears in three scenes and is only ever shown complaining about the weather. She is best described as:
options: the protagonist
a flat character
a round character
a dynamic character
questions.explanation: A flat character is built around a single trait, and here complaining is all we ever see. She is not dynamic, because she does not change, and a figure in only three scenes is not the protagonist. Flat characters are not a weakness; minor roles often need only one clear trait.

questions.stem: What is the difference between a static and a dynamic character?
options: A static character is always a minor one; a dynamic character is always the protagonist
A static character is always bad; a dynamic character is always good, kind and brave
A static character never speaks; a dynamic character has lines of dialogue
A static character stays essentially the same; a dynamic one changes in an important way
questions.explanation: The terms describe change across the story: a dynamic character learns, grows or shifts in attitude, while a static one ends much as they began. A protagonist is often dynamic, but minor characters can change too and a main character can stay static. Neither term says anything about whether a character is good or bad.

questions.stem: Which character is an example of the mentor archetype?
options: A cunning fox who tricks the other animals to get exactly what it wants
A newcomer who never manages to fit in with the town's tight-knit families
A trusting child who believes everyone and sees only good in people
An old fisherman who teaches a girl the skills she needs for her journey
questions.explanation: The mentor is the wise guide who prepares the hero, often an older figure passing on knowledge or tools. The fox is the trickster, the newcomer is the outsider and the trusting child is the innocent, all different archetypes. Spotting archetypes helps you see how a story connects to patterns found across many cultures.

questions.stem: What is the difference between an archetype and a stereotype?
options: An archetype is a character who changes over time; a stereotype is a character who never changes
An archetype is a pattern found across cultures' stories; a stereotype oversimplifies a group
An archetype is an unfair, oversimplified view of a group; a stereotype is a pattern found in myths
An archetype appears only in ancient myths; a stereotype appears only in modern novels and films
questions.explanation: Archetypes such as the hero, the mentor and the trickster recur across stories from many times and places, and writers use them as building blocks. A stereotype reduces a whole group of real people to a fixed, often unfair image. The swapped version is tempting because both terms describe familiar types, but only a stereotype carries that judgement about a group.

questions.stem: In a novel, calm, careful Priya shares most scenes with her reckless, impulsive cousin Jai. Jai mainly acts as her foil, which means he:
options: opposes her as the main villain trying to stop her goals
narrates the story so readers see events through his eyes
is a minor character who has no real effect on the plot
contrasts with her, so her qualities stand out
questions.explanation: A foil is a character whose differences highlight another character's traits, the way a dark background makes a bright colour pop. A foil is not the same as an antagonist: Jai can be her loyal friend and still be her foil. His recklessness makes her caution more visible.

questions.stem: Direct characterisation is when:
options: the narrator tells the reader outright what a character is like
the reader works out a character's traits from what they say and do
a character speaks straight to the audience during a play
a character's name is used as the title of the story
questions.explanation: In direct characterisation the narrator simply states the trait, such as 'Sam was generous'. Working traits out from actions, speech and appearance is indirect characterisation, the 'show, don't tell' approach. Speaking to the audience in a play is an aside or soliloquy, a drama convention.

questions.stem: Which sentence uses indirect characterisation?
options: Sam was generous to a fault, as everyone already knew.
Sam slid the last biscuit onto his sister's plate.
Sam was the most generous person in the whole family.
Sam was a quiet and thoughtful boy who cared for others.
questions.explanation: Indirect characterisation shows a trait through action, speech or thought and lets the reader draw the conclusion, here that Sam is generous and quietly kind. The other sentences all tell the reader the trait outright, which is direct characterisation. Indirect characterisation usually feels more convincing because readers discover it for themselves.

questions.stem: Which order shows the stages of a traditional narrative structure?
options: Climax, exposition, rising action, falling action, resolution
Exposition, rising action, climax, falling action, resolution
Exposition, climax, rising action, resolution, falling action
Rising action, exposition, climax, resolution, falling action
questions.explanation: A traditional plot introduces characters and setting, builds tension through complications, reaches a turning point, then winds down to an ending. The climax must follow the rising action, because tension has to build before it can peak. Many stories play with this order, but this is the pattern they are playing with.

questions.stem: In a story, a girl finds a stray dog, hides it from her strict father, and is nearly caught twice. These events belong to the:
options: resolution
rising action
exposition
falling action
questions.explanation: Rising action is the series of complications that builds tension towards the climax, and each near miss raises the stakes. The exposition would introduce the girl and her situation before the problem starts. Falling action comes after the climax, once the main conflict has turned.

questions.stem: What happens in the denouement of a story?
options: The characters and setting are introduced to readers
Remaining questions are settled and loose ends tied up
The main conflict is introduced for the very first time
Tension reaches its highest and most decisive point
questions.explanation: Denouement is a French word meaning 'untying', and it is the final part of the story, after the climax, when things are settled. The highest point of tension is the climax, which comes before it. Introducing characters and setting happens in the exposition at the start.

questions.stem: A novel follows a boy training for a surfing contest, while a smaller storyline shows his grandmother learning to use a computer. The grandmother's storyline is a:
options: climax
flashback
frame narrative
subplot
questions.explanation: A subplot is a secondary storyline running alongside the main plot, often echoing or contrasting with it. A flashback is a jump back in time, not a separate storyline. A frame narrative is a story told within another story, which is not what is happening here.

questions.stem: A story opens: 'The car was already sliding towards the river when Leah grabbed the wheel.' Starting a story this way is called:
options: a denouement
circular structure
in medias res
a frame narrative
questions.explanation: In medias res is Latin for 'in the middle of things': the story drops the reader into the action and fills in the background later. A denouement is the settling of events at the end, the opposite end of the story. A frame narrative would begin with someone about to tell a story.

questions.stem: A novel begins with an old woman telling her granddaughter, 'Let me tell you about the summer of 1974.' Most of the book is that story, and it ends back with the two of them. This structure is a:
options: subplot
flashforward
frame narrative
parallel narrative
questions.explanation: A frame narrative places one story inside another: the outer story of the grandmother and granddaughter frames the inner story of 1974. Parallel narratives run two storylines side by side, usually alternating, rather than one inside the other. The frame lets readers see how the past still matters to the present.

questions.stem: A novel alternates chapters between a girl in 1942 Darwin and a boy in present-day Darwin, and the two storylines finally connect in the last chapter. What is this structure, and what is a likely effect?
options: Parallel narratives, inviting readers to compare the two lives and look for links
A frame narrative, in which one character tells the other's story aloud to them
A linear narrative, presenting all the events in the order they happened
In medias res, starting the novel at the most exciting moment of the plot
questions.explanation: Parallel narratives run two storylines side by side, so readers naturally compare them and look for how they will meet. It is not a frame narrative, because neither character is telling the other's story. It is not linear either, since the chapters jump back and forth across eighty years.

questions.stem: What is a circular narrative structure?
options: A story that ends where it began, often returning to the opening place or image
A story told in two timelines that alternate with each other chapter by chapter
A story that begins in the middle of the action and explains things later
A story with several narrators who each tell one part of what happened
questions.explanation: A circular structure brings the story back to its starting point, which invites readers to notice how much has changed, or how little. Two alternating timelines make parallel narratives, and starting mid-action is in medias res. Returning to the opening often gives a satisfying sense of completion.

questions.stem: Which story has a non-linear structure?
options: A story told by a narrator who describes events just as they happen
A story that moves steadily from the start of a long journey to its very end
A story that jumps between a man's childhood, wedding and old age
A story that follows one ordinary day from breakfast to bedtime in order
questions.explanation: A non-linear structure presents events out of chronological order, through flashbacks, time jumps or shifting timelines. A day told from breakfast to bedtime is linear even though it is short. Telling events as they happen is a choice about tense and narration, not about the order of events.

questions.stem: In a short story, one sentence covers ten years — 'The decade passed in school runs and night shifts' — while three pages describe a thirty-second car crash. What is the writer doing?
options: Compressing unimportant time and expanding a key moment to build its impact
Telling the events out of order to keep the reader confused about them
Using a frame narrative so that two different storytellers can be heard
Switching from first-person to third-person narration halfway through
questions.explanation: Writers control the pace of time: a summary sentence can race through years, while slowing down to every detail stretches a moment so readers feel it fully. The events here are still in order, so this is not a non-linear structure. Asking where time is stretched shows you what the writer thinks matters most.

questions.stem: A third-person omniscient narrator:
options: can report the thoughts of only one single character
speaks to the reader as you all the way through
can reveal the thoughts of any character at all
is a character in the story who uses I and me
questions.explanation: Omniscient means 'all-knowing', so this narrator can move into any character's mind and know things none of them know. Being limited to one character's thoughts is third-person limited narration. A narrator who uses I and me is a first-person narrator.

questions.stem: 'Ella wondered why her coach would not look at her. Across the oval, the other players whispered, but she could not hear what they said.' What point of view is this?
options: Third-person omniscient, revealing every character's thoughts
First person, told by Ella about herself
Second person, addressing the reader as you
Third-person limited, staying with Ella's knowledge
questions.explanation: The narrator uses 'she' but knows only what Ella knows: we get her wondering, and we cannot hear the whispers either. An omniscient narrator could simply tell us what the coach was thinking and what the players said. The limited view puts readers in the same uncertain position as Ella.

questions.stem: A novel narrated in third person describes a family's house move entirely through what the seven-year-old daughter notices, such as the removalists' tattoos and the empty fridge. In this passage, the daughter is the:
options: narrator
antagonist
foil
focaliser
questions.explanation: The focaliser is the character through whose eyes and mind events are filtered. The daughter is not the narrator, because a third-person narrator is telling the story and she never says 'I'. Separating who speaks (the narrator) from who sees (the focaliser) is the key idea behind focalisation.

questions.stem: In the middle of a story, the narrator stops to say, 'Now, dear reader, you may think Tom deserved what came next — but wait.' This is an example of:
options: narrative intrusion
free indirect speech
a flashback
in medias res
questions.explanation: Narrative intrusion is when the narrator steps out of the story to comment on it or speak directly to the reader. Free indirect speech does the opposite, blending the narrator's voice quietly into a character's thoughts. Intrusion reminds readers that someone is telling them this story.

questions.stem: A poem's speaker says, 'I have never left this town and never will.' The poet actually lives overseas. What is the best explanation?
options: The speaker is the antagonist, so readers should distrust every single line
The speaker is a persona, a voice the poet has created, not the poet herself
The poem must be dishonest, because the speaker of a poem is always the poet
The poem is written in second person, so the speaker is really the reader
questions.explanation: Writers often create a persona, a speaking voice that is a character, just as novelists create narrators. Assuming the 'I' of a poem is always the poet is a common mistake that can lead to misreading. The poem uses 'I', so it is first person, not second person.

questions.stem: Which sentence uses indirect (reported) speech?
options: Mia said that she would be late for training.
'I'll be late for training,' Mia said.
Mia said, 'I'll be late for training.'
'Late again!' Mia groaned, grabbing her training bag.
questions.explanation: Indirect speech reports what someone said without quoting their exact words, so there are no quotation marks and the pronouns and tense shift ('I will' becomes 'she would'). The other sentences quote Mia's actual words inside quotation marks, which is direct speech.

questions.stem: 'Kai stared at the test. Twenty questions, and he knew maybe three. Brilliant. Just brilliant.' What technique do the last sentences show?
options: Direct speech, quoting the words Kai says out loud to his class
Omniscient narration, revealing every student's private thoughts
Narrative intrusion, with the narrator speaking to the reader
Free indirect speech, blending narrator and Kai's thoughts
questions.explanation: Free indirect speech keeps third-person narration but slips into the character's own voice, here Kai's sarcastic 'Brilliant. Just brilliant.' There are no quotation marks, so the words are not spoken aloud as direct speech. The technique lets readers hear a character's mind without leaving the narrator's voice.
